Land Use Land Cover (LULC) map for India. Novelty of this approach is intra-annual classes for agriculture and water availability aligned to the agriculture seasons of India.

The Pan India map is available from 2017 onwards at 10m resolution. These are the classes in the current version of LULC:
1. builtup
2. water in kharif only
3. water in kharif and rabi only
4. water in kharif, rabi and zaid (perennial water)
5. cropland
6. trees and forest
7. barren land
8. single kharif cropping
9. single non-kharif cropping
10. double cropping
11. tripple cropping
12. shrubs and scrubs

Input to the model is Dynamic World output, and timeseries data from Landsat-7, Landsat-8, Sentinel-2, Sentinel-1 and MODIS processed using the IndiaSAT methodology. Details of methodology can be found in our technical manual and the codebase on [github](https://github.com/core-stack-org/core-stack-backend/tree/main/computing/lulc).

Terrain classification map at 30m resolution for India. The map is based on Topographic Position Index (TPI) and slope. The algorithm is based on a landform classification method by The Nature Conservency (https://www.jennessent.com/downloads/TPI-poster-TNC_18x22.pdf), with fine tuning of the thresholds done for Indian landscapes.

The following classes are available in the current version of the map:
1. V-shape river valleys, Deep narrow canyons
2. Lateral midslope incised drainages, Local valleys in plains
3. Upland incised drainages, Stream headwaters
4. U-shape valleys
5. Broad flat areas
6. Broad open slopes
7. Mesa tops
8. Upper Slopes
9. Local ridge/hilltops within broad valleys
10. Lateral midslope drainage divides, Local ridges in plains
11. Mountain tops, high ridges

Input to the model is digital elevation data (SRTM Digital Elevation 30m). Details of methodology can be found in our technical manual and the codebase on [github](https://github.com/core-stack-org/core-stack-backend/tree/main/computing/terrain_descriptor)

This layer shows areas where tree cover has increased during the selected analysis period. It is generated by comparing the first and last three-year land-use composites and highlighting transitions from built-up land, barren land, shrubland, and agriculture into tree cover. This layer represents restoration, natural regeneration, and gains in vegetation cover over time.

Following are the classes in this layer: 
1.Trees → Trees
2.Built Up → Trees
3.Farm → Trees
4.Barren → Trees
5.Scrub Land → Trees

This layer highlights areas where tree cover has been lost during the selected analysis period. It is derived by comparing the first and last three-year land-use composites and identifying transitions from tree cover to built-up land, agricultural land, barren land, or shrubland. It represents deforestation and long-term reduction in forest cover.

Following are the classes in this layer: 
1.Trees → Trees
2.Trees → Built Up
3.Trees → Crops
4.Trees → Barren
5.Trees → Shrubs and Scrubs

This layer shows the expansion of built-up land over the selected analysis period. It is derived by comparing the composite mode of the first three years of the time series with the composite mode of the last three years of the time series. Areas highlighted in this layer represent conversion from vegetation, agricultural land, barren land, or scrub into built-up land, indicating urban growth, infrastructure development, and settlement expansion.

Following are the classes in this layer: 
1.Built Up → Built Up
2.Water → Built Up
3.Trees/Crops → Built Up
4.Barren/Shrubs and Scrubs → Built Up

This layer identifies land degradation over the selected analysis period. It is generated by comparing the first three-year land-use composite with the last three-year land-use composite and highlighting areas where vegetated or productive land classes have shifted into built-up land, barren land, or scrub. This indicates loss of ecological cover, declining land productivity, and landscape stress.

Following are the classes in this layer: 
1.Crops → Crops
2.Crops → Built Up
3.Crops → Barren
4.Crops → Shrubs and Scrubs

This layer represents changes in agricultural land-use intensity over the selected analysis period. It is derived by comparing the first and last three-year land-use composites and identifying shifts among crop-related classes and agricultural states. It helps monitor changes in cultivation patterns, land productivity, and agricultural transformation.

Cropping intensity change layer includes the following transitions: 
1.Double → Single
2.Tripple/annual/perennial → Single
3.Tripple/annual/perennial → Double
4.Single → Double
5.Single → Tripple/annual/perennial
6.Double → Tripple/annual/perennial
7.Single → Single
8.Double → Double
9.Tripple/annual/perennial → Tripple/annual/perennial

Tree canopy cover density (CCD) indicates the density of tree cover in a given area, with higher canopy cover percentages signifying a denser canopy and more shade on the ground and vice versa. The Pan India map (except ACZ 12-15 currently missing due to insufficient data points for training the respective models) is available from 2017 onwards at 25m resolution.

These are the classes in the current version of the map:

1. Class 0: Low density
2. Class 1: High density
3. Class 2: Missing data

Input to the model is Dynamic World output, and timeseries data from Sentinel-2, Sentinel-1 and GEDI as ground truth. Details of methodology can be found in the [technical manual](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1ZxovdpPThkN09cB1TcUYSE2BImI7M3k_/view?pli=1) and the codebase at <https://github.com/Dhruvi-Goyal/Tree-Health-Monitoring/>

Tree canopy height layer describes how tall are trees in a given pixel. It captures the structural height of vegetation and provides a direct measure of forest maturity and vertical growth. Taller canopies generally indicate more developed or less disturbed forest stands, while shorter canopies may reflect regenerating vegetation, degradation, or recent disturbance. The Pan India map (except ACZ 12-15) is available from 2017 onwards at 25m resolution.

These are the classes in the current version of the map:

1. Class 0: Short
2. Class 1: Medium
3. Class 2: Tall
4. Class 3: Missing data

Details of methodology can be found in the [technical manual](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1ZxovdpPThkN09cB1TcUYSE2BImI7M3k_/view?pli=1) and the codebase at <https://github.com/Dhruvi-Goyal/Tree-Health-Monitoring/>

Drainage lines map for India. Drainage lines in hydrology refer to the visible channels through which water flows from higher elevations to lower elevations on the surface of earth such as streams and rivers. The Pan India map of drainage lines has been generated using SRTM DEM V4 data on QGIS (r.stream.extract). The drainage lines are labeled by their Strahler order. Details of methodology can be found in the technical manual. Details of methodology can be found in the technical manual and the codebase on [github](https://github.com/core-stack-org/core-stack-backend/blob/main/computing/misc/drainage_lines.py).

Stream order raster map for India. While drainage lines are essential to plan assets such as check dams located on the drainage lines, it is also important to identify areas outside of the drainage lines that are under the influence of drainage lines. We use digital elevation model (DEM) data that provides pixel level information on the elevation and drainage lines (with stream orders) as inputs to compute stream order rasters. Areas with higher stream orders are those downstream of areas with lower stream orders, and can help identify cropping regions like low-land, mid-land, and up-land. Details of methodology can be found in the technical manual and the codebase on [github](https://github.com/core-stack-org/core-stack-backend/blob/main/computing/misc/).

Distance to upstream drainage line map for India. Spatial indexing technique (e.g. k-d tree) is applied on pixel level digital elevation data (SRTM DEM) to compute the distance of each non-drainage pixel to its nearest upstream drainage line. 
Details of methodology can be found in the technical manual and the codebase on [github](https://github.com/core-stack-org/core-stack-backend/blob/main/computing/misc/).

Catchment area map for India. The catchment area of a point represents the total land area from which rain water drains into that point. The pan-India catchment area map has been built using digital elevation data and r.watershed tool of GRASS GIS to compute flow accumulation. Details of methodology can be found in the technical manual and the codebase on [github](https://github.com/core-stack-org/core-stack-backend/blob/main/computing/misc/).

Runoff accumulation map for India. Pixel-level elevation data, upstream-downstream microwatershed connectivity, drainage lines and pixel-level runoff data is used to compute pixel-level runoff accumulation. Details of methodology can be found in the technical manual and the codebase on github.

Natural depressions map for India. Natural depressions are valuable for planning water structures under MGNREGA as they naturally collect and store water, making them ideal sites for various water conservation interventions. This is computed using pixel level digital elevation data, and r.fill.dir algorithm of GRASS GIS tool. Details of methodology can be found in the technical manual and the codebase on [github](https://github.com/core-stack-org/core-stack-backend/blob/main/computing/misc/).

Composite Land Assessment and Restoration Tool (CLART) is a tool built by the Foundation for Ecological Security (FES) with the goal of empowering rural communities for planning the sites for soil and water conservation measures. This map is intended to reproduce CLART in a reprogrammable/reconfigurable manner to allow dynamic scoring based on community requirements for their landscape. The recharge score is computed as a weighted index based on underlying layers.

The Pan India map has the following classes: 
1. Good recharge 
2. Moderate recharge
3. Regeneration
4. High runoff zone 
5. Surface water harvesting 

Details of methodology can be found in the technical manual and the codebase on [github](https://github.com/core-stack-org/core-stack-backend/tree/main/computing/clart).

Aquifer map for India generated with data from India Water Resources Information System (WRIS) ArcGIS portal. Ground water is the water present beneath the Earth’s surface in rock and soil pore spaces and in the fractures of rock formation. A unit of rock or an unconsolidated deposit is called an aquifer when it can yield a usable quantity of water. 

Based on the hydrogeological characteristics, the entire nation is divided into 14 principal aquifers: 
1. Alluvium
2. Laterite
3. Basalt
4. Sandstone
5. Shale
6. Limestone
7. Granite
8. Schist
9. Quartzite
10. Charnockite
11. Khondalite
12. Banded Gneissic Complex
13. Gneiss
14. Intrusive

Each major aquifer is uniquely identified by its region-specific aquifer properties such as aquifer thickness, specific yield, transmissivity and whether it is an unconfined and confined aquifer.

The stage of groundwater extraction map for India generated from National Compilation on Dynamic Ground Water Resources of India (2022), by Central Ground Water Board, Government of India. Stage of groundwater extraction (SOGE) is defined as the ratio of annual extraction of groundwater resource and annual extractable groundwater resource. 

The Pan India map is available for the years 2011, 2013, 2017, and 2020. The categories in the map currently are: 
1. Safe (<= 70%), 
2. Semi-critical (> 70% and ≤ 90%), 
3. Critical (> 90% and ≤ 100%) and 
4. Over Exploited (> 100%)

Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA) assets categorization map for India. Permissible works under the scheme have been categorized from the natural resource management (NRM) lens through keyword matching, with the goal of helping in examining the current distribution of assets and facilitate the planning of new assets to ensure water security and sustainable livelihoods in rural India. 

The Pan India map is available from 2017 onwards. These are the classes in the current version of the map:
1. Soil and water conservation
2. Irrigation on farms
3. Other on-farm works
4. Plantations
5. Land restoration
6. Off-farm livelihood assets
7. Community assets

Input to the keyword matching algorithm is MGNREGS permissible work list and MGNREGA assets obtained from Bhuvan. Details of methodology can be found in the technical manual and the codebase on [github](https://github.com/core-stack-org/core-stack-backend/blob/main/computing/misc/nrega.py).

Administration boundaries map of India. State and district boundaries data is taken from Survey of India. Administrative block boundaries are generated for 15 states by using village shapefiles from NASA SEDAC website, and village to panchayat mapping obtained from the Local Government Directory data.  Additionally, the village level data is compiled with village level household variables of census 2011 and the Aggregate Development Index (ADI) of 2001, 2011 and 2019. Resolution of villages between 2001 and 2011 is done using SHRUG IDs.
Details of methodology can be found in the technical manual and the codebase on [github](https://github.com/core-stack-org/core-stack-backend/blob/main/computing/misc/admin_boundary.py).

Drought frequency map for India. The Department of Agriculture, Cooperation & Farmers Welfare under the Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare, Government of India released the "Manual for Drought Management" in 2016 for the prevention, mitigation and management of droughts in India. The manual introduces scientific indices and parameters such as Vegetation Condition Index (VCI) for more accurate determination and assessment of drought. This map is an attempt to implement the methodology of the drought manual using various remote sensing products.

Following are the output classes in the model: 
1. Severe
2. Moderate
3. Mild

Input to the model is Rainfall data  (CHIRPS), Vegetation data (Landsat), Crop data (MODIS), Land use land cover (IndiaSAT). Details of methodology can be found in the technical manual and the codebase on [github](https://github.com/core-stack-org/core-stack-backend/tree/main/computing/drought).

Surface water bodies map for India. Surface Water is any body of water above ground, including streams, rivers, and lakes. To generate this map, water pixels from the Land Use Land Cover model (IndiaSAT) for each year are taken and converted into a vector layer. Given the intra annual classes for water availability based on India’s agriculture calendar in IndiaSAT, water availability in each season of the year (kharif, rabi, zaid) for each of the waterbodies is computed. This data is also combined with waterbody census data (2023) to additionally get a capacity map for the waterbodies.  Details of methodology can be found in the technical manual and the codebase on [github](https://github.com/core-stack-org/core-stack-backend/tree/main/computing/surface_water_bodies).

Water balance with fortnightly temporal resolution for India. The vertical flux for a micro-watershed is computed as: Water Balance (ΔG) = Precipitation (P) - Runoff (Qout) - Evapotranspiration (ET). 

Precipitation data has been obtained from JAXA's Global Satellite Mapping of Precipitation (GSMaP), Evapotranspiration data from FLDAS Noah land Surface model by NASA and USGS, and runoff has been computed on a per-pixel using slope-adjusted CN numbers, the hydrological soil group, and LULC. Note that this only computes the vertical flux and does not account for sub-surface flows from adjacent micro-watersheds. 

The vector data contains timeseries of fortnightly mean precipitation (in mm), runoff (in mm), evapotranspiration (in mm), water balance (in mm), and cumulative water balance since 2017 as an indicator of cumulative surplus or deficit, for each microwatershed.

Details of methodology can be found in the technical manual and the codebase on [github](https://github.com/core-stack-org/core-stack-backend/tree/main/computing/mws).

Annual water balance map for India. Data to compute the water balance for each microwatershed as rainfall - evapotranspiration - runoff, along with the specific yield obtained from aquifer data are used to estimate the change in depth to water. Note that this only takes the vertical flux into account and hence is likely to suffer from accuracy issues in the absence of accounting for lateral flow through the underlying aquifer. 

The vector data contains timeseries of annual mean precipitation (in mm), runoff (in mm), evapotranspiration (in mm), water balance (in mm), and cumulative water balance since 2017 as an indicator of cumulative surplus or deficit, for each microwatershed.

Details of methodology can be found in the technical manual and the codebase on [github](https://github.com/core-stack-org/core-stack-backend/blob/main/computing/mws/well_depth.py).

Cropping intensity map for India. Cropping intensity is computed on the IndiaSAT Land Use Land Cover outputs by taking the weighted average of the area under single cropping, double cropping, and tripple/annual/perennial cropping. The vector map is available from 2017 onwards. Details of methodology can be found in the technical manual and the codebase on [github](https://github.com/core-stack-org/core-stack-backend/tree/main/computing/cropping_intensity).

Landscape restoration opportunities map built by World Resources Institute (WRI) identifies the potential for protection, wide-scale restoration, and mosaic restoration in India. 
Following classes are available in the raster map:

1. Protection: Protection areas have forest cover with a density of more than 40 percent.
2. Wide scale restoration: Areas suitable for wide-scale restoration are those where near contiguous tracts of forest and tree cover can be established. The existing tree density in these areas is less than 40 percent and the population density is less than 200 persons per square kilometre.
3. Mosaic restoration: Mosaic restoration is the integration of trees in a patchwork of different land uses including rainfed cultivated areas. These areas have tree cover density of less than 40 percent and population density of less than 400 persons per sq.km. 

Details of the datasets used and the methodology can be found at [india.restorationatlas.org](https://india.restorationatlas.org/)

Terrain clusters map for India. Classes in the terrain raster map are grouped into five broad categories: plains, broad slopes, steep slopes, valleys and ridges. Percentage area under each category is computed for each microwatershed. Clustering process was applied to microwatersheds across diverse terrain blocks, including: Masalia, Angul, Mandalgarh, Pindwara, Mohanpur. The identified clusters are: 

1. Broad sloppy and hilly
2. Mostly plains
3. Mostly hills and valleys
4. Broad plains and slopes

Precomputed cluster centroids are used to assign terrain clusters to new microwatersheds. Details of methodology can be found in the technical manual and the codebase on [github](https://github.com/core-stack-org/core-stack-backend/tree/main/computing/terrain_descriptor).
Map of per pixel slope computed from digital elevation data (SRTM DEM).

Map of microwatershed connectivity for India. Each microwatershed has a single pour point as its outlet connecting to a downstream micro-watershed but can receive inflow from multiple upstream micro-watersheds. Pour point of each micro-watershed has been determined using flow accumulation and then mapped to its downstream microwatershed to which it flows, resulting in a microwatershed connectivity network in a basin. Details of methodology can be found in the [technical manual](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1ZxovdpPThkN09cB1TcUYSE2BImI7M3k_/view)

Stream order vector map for India. While drainage lines are essential to plan assets such as check dams located on the drainage lines, it is also important to identify areas outside of the drainage lines that are under the influence of drainage lines. We use digital elevation model (DEM) data that provides pixel level information on the elevation and drainage lines (with stream orders) as inputs to compute stream order. Areas with higher stream orders are those downstream of areas with lower stream orders, and can help identify cropping regions like low-land, mid-land, and up-land. Details of methodology can be found in the technical manual and the codebase on [github](https://github.com/core-stack-org/core-stack-backend/blob/main/computing/misc/).

This vector layer summarizes the area of tree cover gain within the selected MWS boundary over the analysis period. It is created by comparing the first and last three-year IndiaSAT land-use composites and aggregating the identified transitions to the MWS boundary. The output highlights conversions from built-up land, barren land, shrubland, and agricultural land into tree cover, indicating restoration, regeneration, and natural recovery within the planning unit.

This vector layer summarizes changes in agricultural land-use intensity within the selected MWS boundary over the analysis period. It is generated from IndiaSAT Land Use and Land Cover composites by comparing the first and last three-year composites and aggregating the crop-related class transitions to the MWS boundary. The output captures shifts among agricultural classes and helps quantify changes in cultivation intensity and land productivity within the study area.

This vector layer summarizes the area of tree cover loss within the selected MWS boundary over the analysis period. It is derived from IndiaSAT Land Use and Land Cover composites by comparing the first three-year composite with the last three-year composite and aggregating the detected transitions to the MWS boundary. The output represents conversion from tree cover to built-up land, agricultural land, barren land, or shrubland, indicating deforestation within the planning unit.

This vector layer summarizes the area affected by land degradation within the selected MWS boundary over the analysis period. It is generated from IndiaSAT Land Use and Land Cover composites by comparing the first and last three-year composites and aggregating the detected transitions to the MWS boundary. The output captures pixels where vegetated or productive land classes changed into built-up land, barren land, or scrub, indicating loss of ecological cover and declining land productivity.

This vector layer summarizes the area of built-up land expansion within the selected MWS boundary over the analysis period. It is derived from IndiaSAT Land Use and Land Cover composites by comparing the first three-year composite with the last three-year composite and aggregating the resulting land-cover transitions to the MWS boundary. Areas included in this output represent conversion from vegetation, agricultural land, barren land, or scrub into built-up land, indicating urban growth and settlement expansion within the planning unit.

This Layer helps us to get the proximity of 25 types of nearest facilities from each of the villages across India. The data was downloaded from multiple resources, primarily on Gram Manchitra. Distances of a village (from its centroid) to the nearest facility was computed offline to build the final [dataset](https://drive.google.com/file/d/10vwjga8friz5kaTRAD-3VzNNBbRczaOY/view)

The plantation site suitability layer is built using a GIS-based assessment to identify regions ideal for agroforestry to combat land degradation and soil erosion, using a Multi-Criteria Analysis (MCA) framework that integrates 24 environmental and socioeconomic variables across five thematic criteria - Climate (default weight: 35%), Topography (25%), Soil (20%), Ecology (10%), and Socioeconomic Factors (10%) - each of which is itself a weighted mean of its underlying variables. These variables are reclassified into suitability classes and combined using a Weighted Overlay method. The final score per pixel ranges from 1 (Very Good) to 5 (Unsuitable): 

 - Climate: annual precipitation, mean annual temperature, aridity index, reference evapotranspiration. 
 - Topography: elevation, slope, aspect. 
 - Soil: topsoil and subsoil pH, organic carbon, cation exchange capacity (CEC), texture, bulk density, drainage class, and available water capacity (AWC). 
 - Ecology: NDVI (canopy greenness) and LULC forest cover (prioritising barren or sparsely forested land). 
 - Socioeconomic Factors: proximity to roads, settlements, and drainage networks. 

Weights are configurable at the criterion, subcriterion, and variable level. The layer can be generated for any user-defined region of interest via the CoRE Stack Dashboard.

Dataset of land parcels registered under India's Green Credit Programme (GCP) sourced from the MoEFCC Green Credit Registry - [Land Inventory Portal](https://www.moefcc-gcp.in/registry/land-inventory).
Each feature represents a land parcel available for afforestation or ecosystem restoration, administered by forest departments at the state and district level. Parcel boundaries are derived from KML files published on the registry and are suitable for restoration planning, ecological indicator computation (tree cover gain, soil type, proximity to settlements), and integration into landscape restoration applications.

The dataset is derived from the Annual Survey of Industries (ASI) 2018 data frame by the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MOSPI), Government of India. It contains information on registered industrial units across Indian districts, including details like state, district, industry code (NIC 2008), total persons engaged, and factory name. Geographic coordinates were obtained by geocoding the address. Suitable for spatial analysis of industrial presence, workforce distribution, proximity-based assessments, and binary filtering of villages or planning units by factory presence.

Dataset created by the Consortium of Agroecological Transformation (CAT) of organisations actively engaged in agroecological practices, representing civil society organisations, non-profits, and grassroots groups working across rural blocks and districts. Contains information about the organisation's operational location and includes attributes such as organisation name, type, the agroecological domains they work in (e.g. cultivation practices, soil conservation, livestock management, seed management, watershed management), contact details, and the date of registration. Suitable for mapping civil society presence, identifying agroecological practice coverage, and supporting planning of landscape restoration initiatives.

This layer contains high-resolution (30m) raster maps of predicted soil nutrients and organic carbon across India. Separate raster layers are generated for nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), potassium (K), and organic carbon (OC) using machine learning and satellite remote sensing, trained on data aggregated by the governments from soil health card tests for the 2023–24 agricultural period. An additional organic carbon layer from the OpenLandMap (OLM) baseline is provided for comparison. Soil health is a foundational indicator for agricultural resilience, land degradation assessment, and precision farming interventions.

The raster layers are clipped to the selected microwatershed area to retain the relevant spatial extent.

- N, P and K: Reported in kg/ha and masked on crop pixels of IndiSAT LULC.
- OC and OC_OLM: Reported in percent (%) and masked on tree and shrub pixels of IndiSAT LULC.
- Each pixel represents the predicted soil property value for that location.
- OC_OLM: Represents the OpenLandMap organic carbon baseline used for comparison with the custom Random Forest predictions. It is not an estimate specifically for tree- and shrub-covered areas.

Following are the classes in this layer:

1. Shrub → Shrub
2. Shrub → Farm
3. Shrub → Tree
4. Shrub → Built-up

This vector layer summarizes changes in shrub and scrub-dominated areas within the selected MWS boundary over the analysis period. It is derived from IndiaSAT Land Use and Land Cover composites by comparing the first and last three-year composites and aggregating the detected transitions to the MWS boundary. The output captures changes from shrubland into tree cover, agriculture, built-up land, water, and barren land, as well as persistence of shrub cover, indicating vegetation dynamics in non-forest and transitional landscapes.

This layer contains one feature for each microwatershed. The clipped soil health rasters are used to calculate statistics for each microwatershed, summarising the spatial distribution of predicted soil nutrients and organic carbon within the selected microwatershed.

The vector layer includes the mean and percentile statistics for nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, and organic carbon, along with the corresponding valid pixel counts. Where applicable, the OpenLandMap organic carbon baseline can also be included for comparison.

- N, P and K statistics: Reported in kg/ha.
- OC and OC_OLM statistics: Reported in percent (%).
- Mean: Average predicted soil property value across valid raster pixels within the microwatershed.
- Percentiles: 5th, 10th, 20th, 30th, 40th, 50th, 60th, 70th, 80th, 90th and 95th, where available in the output.
- Pixel count: Number of valid raster pixels used to calculate the statistics for each soil property.

The Soil Type / Soil Variables layer provides essential spatial datasets on the physical, chemical, and hydrological properties of soil across India. These datasets draw from the global dataset of the Harmonized World Soil Database (HWSD v1.2).

Key Components & Sub-Layers

- Soil Texture & Depth Profiles: Topsoil (0–30 cm) and subsoil (30–100 cm) texture classes based on sand, silt, and clay proportions using USDA classifications.
- Chemical & Physical Health: Measures topsoil and subsoil pH (acidity/alkalinity), Organic Carbon (OC), Bulk Density (compaction), and Cation Exchange Capacity (CEC) to determine nutrient storage and soil health.
- Hydrologic Soil Groups (HSGs): Categorizes soils into Groups A, B, C, and D based on infiltration rates and runoff potential.
- Drainage & Water Capacity: Details Soil Drainage Classes (ranging from excessively to very poorly drained) and Available Water Capacity (AWC) in mm/m for plant water uptake.

This layer quantifies forest-edge degradation by measuring how much deforestation and degradation occurred in a 50 m fringe around stable forest patches inside each micro-watershed. Monitoring changes in forest fringes is critical for understanding its implications for ecosystem health and livestock-dependent livelihoods.

Unlike dense forest systems, tree degradation in grasslands is more subtle and spatially fragmented, making it difficult to detect using conventional approaches.

To address this, we introduce a contextual and transition-based framework to monitor tree degradation within grassland ecosystems. By combining temporally smoothed Land Use Land Cover (LULC) data with neighbourhood-based classification, we identify trees within grassland contexts and track their transitions over time. This enables the detection of tree degradation such as conversion to barren land, cropland, or built-up areas.

Detection and monitoring of forest fires is critical for understanding ecosystem disturbances, carbon emissions, and risks to forest-dependent livelihoods. To characterize the spatial and temporal variability of fire activity, the analysis uses satellite-derived Fire Radiative Power (FRP) and fire-day observations. Fire intensity and fire frequency are summarized at the microwatershed level using annualized and multi-year fire indicators.

Livestock are a central part of the rural economy -- a store of savings, insurance against crop failure, a daily income through milk, and a livelihood base for landless and marginal households. The Livestock Census, conducted periodically by the Department of Animal Husbandry and Dairying together with the State Governments and Union Territories, is the principal source of livestock data in the country. This layer publishes village-level headcounts from the 20th Livestock Census (reference year 2019) for the five major species groups -- cattle, buffalo, sheep, goat, and pig. It complements the land, water, and facilities layers, since grazing pressure bears on commons and watershed health, livestock water demand matters for water budgeting, and dairy and meat production potential depends on the local livestock mix.

This layer shows the area surrounding each waterbody that may be influenced by it for soil moisture enrichment. The ZOI is represented as a circular buffer around the waterbody’s centre, with its size estimated from the waterbody’s area. Each feature includes the waterbody ID, ZOI radius, and estimated ZOI area.

NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index) is computed over cropped areas in the microwatersheds at 14-day intervals using satellite data, and reflects the vigour of vegetation/crop growth over time.
NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index) is computed over shrub areas in the microwatersheds at 14-day intervals using satellite data. It reflects changes in shrub vegetation vigour over time.

NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index) is computed over tree-covered areas in the microwatershed at 14-day intervals using satellite data, and reflects the vigour of tree/forest growth over time.

These metrics are derived from the Government of India-led Mission Antyodaya Survey, carried out across India between 2018-2020, collecting village-level data on a wide range of indicators related to areas like health, education, infrastructure, economic activity, etc.

The tree cover change layer describes the change in canopy cover density (CCD) and canopy height (CH) across different years. The Pan India map (except ACZ 12-15 currently missing due to insufficient data points for training the respective models) is available from 2017 onwards at 25m resolution.

The following classes are available in the current version of the map:

1. Class -2: Tree cover lost (tree cover to no tree cover)
2. Class -1: Degradation (reduction in CCD/CH)
3. Class 0: No Change
4. Class 1: Improvement (increase in CCD/CH)
5. Class 2: Tree cover gained (no tree cover to tree cover)
6. Class 3: Partially Degraded (increase in CCD and reduction in CH)
7. Class 4: Partially Degraded (increase in CH and reduction in CCD)
8. Class 5: Missing Data

Details of methodology can be found in the technical manual and the codebase on [GitHub](https://github.com/Dhruvi-Goyal/Tree-Health-Monitoring/).

This vector layer summarizes the area occupied by different canopy density classes within the selected MWS boundary. It is generated by aggregating the pixel-level tree canopy cover density (CCD) raster into area statistics, so each boundary contains the total area under low-density canopy, high-density canopy, and missing-data regions. It is used to quantify how much area within a planning unit falls into each canopy density category.

This vector layer summarizes the distribution of canopy height classes within the selected MWS boundary. It is derived by aggregating the tree canopy height raster to area-based statistics, enabling estimation of how much area falls under short, medium, tall, or missing-data canopy height classes. It is useful for understanding the structural maturity of tree cover and the relative dominance of short versus tall vegetation within a planning unit.

This vector layer summarizes the area affected by tree cover change within the selected MWS boundary. It is generated by aggregating the pixel-level tree cover change raster to the boundary, so each polygon reports how much area has experienced loss, degradation, improvement, gain, or missing-data conditions. This layer is useful for area-based reporting of forest condition changes and helps quantify the extent of canopy decline or recovery within a planning unit.

The Drought Causality layer is a yearly vector layer computed at the microwatershed scale. It is designed to identify the specific triggers and ecological/agricultural impacts of drought events, empowering rural communities to select targeted climate adaptation strategies. A year is declared a drought year for a microwatershed when it records more than 5 weeks of moderate or severe drought during the monsoon.

The layer combines meteorological triggers with impact indicators, all assessed week by week through the monsoon. The triggers are:

- Rainfall deviation from long-period averages,
- Dry spells (4 consecutive weeks, each with a rainfall deficit above 50%),
- The Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI).

The impact indicators are:

- The Vegetation Condition Index (VCI), from NDVI and NDWI,
- The Moisture Adequacy Index (MAI), the ratio of Actual Evapotranspiration (AET) to Potential Evapotranspiration (PET),
- The percentage of Kharif crop area sown.

Each moderate or severe drought week is mapped to its combination of trigger and impact. In declared drought years, these combinations are tallied to find the top three cause-and-impact pairs for each micro-watershed.

The results point to different responses:

- Rainfall-driven droughts suggest rainwater harvesting structures.
- Soil moisture decline suggests changing cropping patterns or adopting drought resistant crops.
- Crop health loss and reduced sown area signal severe agricultural impact, calling for longer-term strategies such as livelihood diversification.
